newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Refugees in Tanzania report fresh fighting in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Refugees in Tanzania report fresh fighting in Zaire.

text.p: Ethnic Tutsi Zairean rebels are engaged in fresh fighting with local people around Fizi in South Kivu, refugees who fled the fighting by boat to Tanzania said on Saturday.
More than 40,000 Zairean refugees have arrived in Tanzania's western Kigoma region this month, the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) said.
Refugees and aid workers say the ethnic Tutsi rebels who control much of Eastern Zaire are fighting members of the Mbembe tribe.
"The Banyamulenge, we stayed with them, but now they've changed their mentality about us. It's the Banyamulenge against the people of Fizi," said Wlongo, 33, a Zairean and former church official.
"The Banyamulenge tribe want to seize this area, the situation is bad, we are many people here from Fizi and many more people want to cross the lake," he said.
"The rebels are coming down and attacking villages and the Zairean army is doing the same so these refugees are really running away from both groups," said an aid worker who interviewed new arrivals.
However, other refugees said the Zairean army had fled the area. Fizi is 200 km (125 miles) south of Bukavu.

"They (refugees) say the war is still going on between the Banyamulenge and local youths, they tell us the youths have taken up arms because the Zairean army has run away," said Malik Aziz, an official with the World Vision agency.
Refugees from the Mbembe tribe around Fizi are also arriving, saying they were fleeing the Banyamulenge.
More than 40,000 Zaireans arrived at Kigoma port between November 1 and 20, according to UNHCR statistics.
At the same time 38,925 Burundians who fled fighting in the country's south eastern provinces have fled to Kibondo this month and 10,225 have fled to Kasulu, both places north of Kigoma.
Thousands of unregistered refugees are thought to be still located in villages around Kigoma on the shores of Lake Tanganyika, said John Adu, head of mission for UNHCR in Kigoma.
"We are bringing more trucks from Ngara and Uganda to move them out of town," said Adu. Transport was the biggest problem the aid agencies faced, he said.
"When the refugees arrive we separate the Zaireans from the Burundians and put the Burundians at camps in Kasulu and Kibondo," he added.
At Kibilizi Port in Kigoma abut 1,000 refugees are arriving by boat every day after collection by UNHCR from villages north of Kigoma along Lake Tanganyika from Eastern Zaire.

"No one seems to have heard of this crisis, all they seem to know is refugees are going home from Goma -- here they are arriving," said Mike Ewing, a U.S. aid official for the Baptist mission based in Kigoma.
